about: Corin is a man whose name is followed, five times, by a 'she' that belongs to a woman the sentence leaves unnamed (the nurse, the aunt, the cook, the neighbour, the girl); his own pronouns are 'he' nine times. A model that cites those windows ends with FEMALE verified; the code's tally is mixed.
title: The Night Ward
author: Ada Pell

chapters.title: Night
paragraphs: Corin carried the tray to the nurse. She thanked him and went on folding sheets.
The ward was quiet in the early hours. Rain ticked against the long windows.
Corin sat on the low stool by the stove. He warmed his hands and watched the kettle.
Mara came in from the yard with a basket of apples. She set it on the table and counted them twice.
Corin opened the ledger. He read the day's entries aloud, slowly, to nobody in particular.
Corin passed the bread to his aunt. She broke it in two and gave half back.
Mara wiped the counter and hummed. She had a way of humming that made the room feel smaller.
Corin walked down to the river before noon. He stood on the old bridge for a long while.
A cart rattled over the stones. The driver lifted his hat and drove on.
Corin handed the keys to the cook. She weighed them in her palm and nodded.
Mara said nothing about the letter. She folded it into her sleeve and went to find the broom.
Corin repaired the shutter by lamplight. He worked without hurry and did not look up.
Corin asked the neighbour about the missing hens. She shrugged and pointed at the hill.
By evening the wind had turned. Smoke from the chimney lay flat along the roof.
Corin lit the lamps one by one. He counted the flames under his breath.
Mara laid the table for four. She put the good cups out, though nobody had said why.
Corin carried the empty pails back to the girl from the mill. She took them without a word.
The night shift came on at nine. Corin gave his report and hung up his coat.
Corin stayed to bank the fire. He stirred the ash and watched it settle.
Mara closed the shutters against the cold. She stood a moment with her hand on the latch.
Corin walked home by the lane. He whistled the old song and lost the tune at the gate.
At the end of the lane Corin met the postman. He nodded and handed over a single card.
Corin read the card twice. He put it in his pocket and said nothing to anyone.
Mara waited at the door with the lamp. She held it high until the lane was empty.
In the district everyone knew Corin, and nobody had a bad word for Corin.
Years afterwards people still asked about Corin, though few could say why.
In the district everyone knew Mara, and nobody had a bad word for Mara.
Years afterwards people still asked about Mara, though few could say why.
